summary: Gives guidance on using external pre-shared keys (PSKs) with TLS 1.3. It lists the security properties PSKs can provide under certain assumptions, shows how breaking those assumptions leads to attacks, and offers advice for applications. It also covers PSK use cases and how keys are provisioned. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A secret password shared ahead of time can lock a conversation, but only if it is truly secret and well chosen. This document explains the pitfalls and how to use such passwords safely.

subtitle: When a secret agreed in advance can safely secure TLS 1.3, and the rules for keeping it safe.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.3 can authenticate with keys provisioned out of band, but nothing told applications how to choose and manage those keys without weakening TLS.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains that PSK security assumes each key is known to exactly one client and one server, shows attacks that follow when a key is shared or has low entropy, and gives four recommendations for applications.
tldr.outcome: Use PSKs of at least 128 bits, combine them with an ephemeral key exchange, keep each one to two logical nodes, and use external PSK importers.

today: RFC 9257 is an Informational RFC from July 2022 from the IETF. The unit metadata shows no RFC obsoletes or updates it. It works together with RFC 9258, which defines external PSK importers.

sections.title: Scope: External PSKs in TLS
sections.content:
External PSKs are symmetric secret keys given to a TLS implementation as external inputs and provisioned out of band. This guidance covers TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) and also applies to DTLS 1.3 (RFC 9147) and Compact TLS 1.3. The RFC uses "TLS" for all of them.

TLS 1.3 also uses PSKs for session resumption, and it distinguishes those resumption PSKs from external ones. There are many resources on password generation, but the RFC notes there was no equivalent for external PSKs in TLS, and aims to reduce that gap.
sections.plainLanguage: Two computers can agree on a secret before they ever talk. This document is the rulebook for using that secret well.

sections.title: What PSKs Give and What They Do Not
sections.content:
A previously established PSK lets TLS nodes authenticate the endpoint identities. It also resists attacks by quantum computers. It does not give privacy protection of endpoint identities, and it does not give non-repudiation, meaning one endpoint can deny the conversation.

All of this rests on one assumption: each PSK is known to exactly one client and one server, and they never switch roles. If that is violated, the security properties of TLS are severely weakened.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared secret proves who you are talking to, as long as only the two of you know it. It does not hide who is talking.

sections.title: Sharing and Weak Keys
sections.content:
If many clients or servers share one PSK, TLS authenticates only group membership. Any member can impersonate any other. If the PSK is not combined with a fresh ephemeral key exchange, compromise of any member lets an attacker read all traffic, including past traffic. Revoking one member also requires a new PSK for everyone else.

A malicious non-member can also reroute handshakes between honest members. With peers A, B and C all holding the PSK, A sends a ClientHello meant for B, the attacker redirects it to C, and C answers A. A finishes the handshake believing it spoke to B. This identity misbinding attack gives no peer authentication, and the Selfie attack is a special case. Checking the Server Name Indication against the member's known identity is a partial mitigation.

Entropy matters too. With a high-entropy PSK, PSK-only modes give the expected properties but lack forward security. With a low-entropy PSK, PSK-only modes face passive exhaustive search, and PSK-DH modes face active attacks. Low-entropy keys are only secure against active attack if a Password-Authenticated Key Exchange (PAKE) is used with TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: If a whole class shares one secret password, anyone in the class can pretend to be anyone else. And a password that is easy to guess is not much of a secret.

sections.title: Use Cases and Provisioning
sections.content:
The RFC lists pairwise use cases: device-to-device links with out-of-band keys, intra-data-center traffic (often to support early data), certificateless server-to-server links, constrained IoT devices, securing RADIUS with TLS, 3GPP authentication, smart cards such as the German eID card, and quantum resistance. Group uses include group chats and IoT fleets that share one key.

Provisioning varies. Some industrial protocols have people type the PSK into a device or use trust on first use. Some devices sync PSKs through a cloud service, and some secrets are baked into hardware or software, even printed on labels. The RFC advises avoiding sharing a PSK between nodes whenever possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Smart cards, sensors and servers all use shared secrets. The hard part is getting the secret into each device safely.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC gives four requirements for applications using external PSKs.

  • Each PSK SHOULD come from at least 128 bits of entropy, MUST be at least 128 bits long, and SHOULD be combined with an ephemeral key exchange, for example the psk_dhe_ke mode, for forward secrecy.
  • Unless other accommodations are made, each PSK MUST be restricted to at most two logical nodes: one client and one server.
  • Nodes SHOULD use external PSK importers (RFC 9258) for a client-server pair.
  • Where possible, the main PSK fed into the importer SHOULD be deleted after the imported keys are generated.

For TLS stack behavior, the RFC notes that PSK identities are opaque bytes of 1 to 65535 bytes in TLS 1.3, compared byte by byte, and that resumption PSK identities SHOULD be assigned so they can be told apart from external ones to avoid collisions.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick a long, random secret. Share it with only one partner. Mix in a fresh secret each time. Then throw away the master copy.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
TLS does little to keep PSK identities private. The identifier appears in cleartext in the ClientHello, so a passive adversary can link connections that use the same external PSK, and may be able to identify the device, person or enterprise behind a client or server. An active attacker can use the identity to block, delay or rate-limit traffic from a specific device.

PSK receivers can also link successive connections that use the same PSK. The RFC treats mitigating these risks as out of scope. It also notes that when early data is used with an external PSK that is reused, the ClientHello random value is the only source of entropy between sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: The name tag on the secret is shown in the open, so someone watching can tell it is the same two friends talking again.
